why: Why a strict single-pass sequence fails in practice follows from what each model's feedback structure is.
Scrum's roles are a closed defined list; 'Tester' is wrong only for not being on it.
The defining trait matches the model's own meaning; no separate fact needs recalling.
Change-responsiveness over plan follows from what Agile is versus plan-driven models.
Iterative and RAD are both feedback-driven by concept, so only the textbook's labelling separates them.
Product-name recall against invented look-alike tool names.
Blueprint-and-specialise follows directly from what classes and inheritance are.
Independence of modules reasons straight to high cohesion plus low coupling.
'Predictable' is a label in a named risk taxonomy; the word itself gives no clue over the alternatives.
Actors-and-roles is what a use case is, so the diagram type follows from the concept.
Scope creep is the predictable consequence of low planning plus constant user change; the distractors invert RAD's own traits.
Arrowhead and diamond shapes are arbitrary notation conventions with no derivation path.
'Open for extension, closed for modification' is reasoned from the principle itself.
Composition vs aggregation turns on the lifetime dependency, which follows from the whole-part idea.
Controlling and documenting a change is what a change-control workflow is, distinguishable from revision tracking by reasoning.
Acronym expansion; the alternatives are equally sensible English and only convention picks one.
Refactoring vs reengineering vs revision is vocabulary discrimination, not a distinction the concepts themselves force.
Central deployment implying one live version is a reasoned trade-off; the stem is ambiguous between two defensible options.
Reasoning about which notation shows objects and relationships, but the stem is OCR-damaged and its intent uncertain.
UML's breadth over any single narrower modelling purpose follows from what a general modelling language is for.
Continuous user involvement follows from how each model gathers feedback, not from a list.
The benefits are all reasoned from incremental delivery; which combination the key accepts is arbitrary, so the label is soft.
Inexperience means risk, and explicit per-cycle risk analysis is what the Spiral model is.
Reasoning about which phase precedes design, but the stem is loosely worded and the intended phase is inferred.
Selecting from a textbook's enumerated design-process activities; the odd item is wrong only for not being listed.
Booch's named property set is an enumeration; which bucket inheritance and aggregation fall into is its convention.
Distinguishing a primary responsibility from its by-products is reasoning about the role, not recall.
Three arbitrarily named ASD phases; nothing about adaptive development yields those particular words.
Static/dynamic bucketing of UML diagram types is a textbook categorisation that does not follow cleanly from the diagrams themselves.
Iteration versus single-pass ordering follows from how OO understanding is refined, not from a recalled definition.
Each listed aim is recognisably part of managing change, so the umbrella answer is reasoned.
Acquiring another class's properties is what inheritance means; the distractors are different mechanisms.
DFD symbol-to-element mapping is an arbitrary notation convention.
Between-elements versus within-element distinguishes coupling from cohesion by definition.
The term follows from the description, but three options are unrelated fragments from a defective print.
The what-not-how boundary of a requirements document rules the odd item out by reasoning.
Each activity is matched to a phase by what the phase does; no list membership is involved.
Independent modifiability reasons directly to high cohesion with low coupling.
'Predictable risk' is a taxonomy label; the alternatives are equally plausible words without the textbook's split.
